note: Government round 3 (part A): concepts and institutions - basic concepts, forms, systems and structures of government, arms of government, constitution, democratic principles, citizenship, ideologies, legislation, elections, parties, pressure groups, public opinion, civil service, public corporations and local government, with an election-results table and a state assembly seats table as data passages.

passages.title: Results of a presidential election in a federation of six states
passages.text:
The table shows the results of a
presidential election in a federation of
six states. The constitution provides that
the winner must score the highest number
of votes and at least one-quarter of the
votes in at least two-thirds of the
states. There were 40 million registered
voters and 25 million valid votes were
cast.

Candidate  Votes (m)  States with 25%+
Adamu        10.5            6
Bello         9.8            3
Chika         3.2            1
Dada          1.5            0

passages.title: Seats won in a 40-member state House of Assembly
passages.text:
The table shows the seats won by four
parties in an election to a state House of
Assembly of 40 members. A simple majority
of members is needed to pass ordinary
bills and a two-thirds majority is needed
to remove the governor.

Party   Seats won
P          14
Q          12
R           8
S           6

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the candidate to be declared winner under the constitution is
questions.A: Bello, who scored 25% in only three states
questions.B: Adamu, who scored the highest votes and 25% in all six states
questions.C: Adamu, because he scored more than half of all the votes
questions.D: nobody, so a fresh election must be held
questions.explanation: Adamu has the highest votes and at least a quarter of the votes in six states, more than the two-thirds (four states) required.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the percentage of the valid votes won by Adamu is
questions.explanation: Adamu's share of the valid votes = 10.5 ÷ 25 × 100 = 42%.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the turnout of registered voters who cast valid votes was
questions.explanation: 25 million valid votes out of 40 million registered voters = 62.5%.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: If the constitution of the federation in the table above had required an absolute majority, the result would have been
questions.A: victory for Adamu at the first ballot
questions.B: a run-off (second ballot) between Adamu and Bello
questions.C: victory for Bello because of his spread of votes
questions.D: a fresh election involving all four candidates
questions.explanation: An absolute majority is more than 50% of the votes; Adamu's 42% falls short, so the two leading candidates go to a second ballot.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The requirement in the table above that the winner must score 25% of the votes in two-thirds of the states is designed to
questions.A: make it impossible for any candidate to win at the first ballot
questions.B: guarantee that the largest state decides the winner
questions.C: ensure that the President has support spread across the federation
questions.D: reduce the number of registered voters in small states
questions.explanation: The geographical spread requirement prevents a candidate from winning on the strength of one region alone.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, if Bello's supporters claim that Adamu did not win an absolute majority, the correct constitutional response is that
questions.A: the legislature must meet in a joint session to choose between Adamu and Bello
questions.B: Adamu must resign at once and hand over the office to Bello as the runner-up
questions.C: the election must be cancelled and a completely fresh election held for all candidates
questions.D: the constitution requires only a plurality plus geographical spread, which Adamu met
questions.explanation: Under the stated rule the winner needs the highest votes (a plurality) and the 25% spread, not more than half of all votes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the party system operating in the state is best described as
questions.A: a two-party system
questions.B: a multi-party system
questions.C: a one-party system
questions.D: a dominant-party system
questions.explanation: Four parties won seats and none has an overall majority, the mark of a multi-party system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the smallest coalition of two parties that can pass an ordinary bill is
questions.A: Q and R, with 20 seats
questions.B: P and S, with 20 seats
questions.C: P and R, with 22 seats
questions.D: R and S, with 14 seats
questions.explanation: A simple majority of 40 members is at least 21 seats; of the pairs listed only P + R (22 seats) reaches it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, the minimum number of members needed to remove the governor is
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 40 is 26.67, so at least 27 members must vote for removal.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, which combination of parties could remove the governor on its own?
questions.A: P and Q together
questions.B: P, Q and R together
questions.C: Q, R and S together
questions.D: P and R together
questions.explanation: P + Q + R = 34 seats, above the 27 needed; P + Q = 26 and Q + R + S = 26 both fall one seat short; P + R = 22.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The situation shown in the table above, where no single party controls the House, is usually described as
questions.A: a landslide victory
questions.B: a one-party state
questions.C: a hung legislature
questions.D: a dictatorship of the majority
questions.explanation: A hung legislature has no party with an overall majority, so coalitions or agreements are needed to govern.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: From the table above, if Party P forms the government with the support of Party R, the party most likely to lead the opposition is
questions.A: P
questions.B: S
questions.C: R
questions.D: Q
questions.explanation: The largest party outside the governing coalition normally leads the opposition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Government as an academic field of study is concerned with
questions.A: the study of rocks, rivers and the climate of a country
questions.B: the institutions, processes and ideas by which societies are ruled
questions.C: the buying and selling of goods and services
questions.D: the keeping of financial records of the state
questions.explanation: As a subject, Government (political science) studies political institutions, behaviour, ideas and processes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A country's government is described as an institution of the state because it
questions.A: cannot be changed once it has been formed
questions.B: owns all the land within the territory of the state
questions.C: is the machinery through which the will of the state is carried out
questions.D: consists only of the armed forces of the state
questions.explanation: The state is permanent and abstract; the government is the agency that makes and enforces its decisions and can change.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following distinguishes a state from a government?
questions.A: the government has territory while the state has none
questions.B: the government has a population while the state does not
questions.C: the state is elected while the government is appointed
questions.D: the state is permanent while governments come and go
questions.explanation: Nigeria has remained one state since 1960 while many governments have ruled it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa are each described as a nation rather than a state because each
questions.A: has a clearly defined territory and an independent government recognised by other states
questions.B: shares a common language and culture but lacks a sovereign government of its own
questions.C: is recognised as a full member of the United Nations and the African Union
questions.D: has its own currency, armed forces and diplomatic missions in other countries
questions.explanation: A nation is a people bound by common culture and identity; a state adds a defined territory, government and sovereignty.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The four essential elements of a state are
questions.A: president, legislature, judiciary and parties
questions.B: army, police, courts and prisons
questions.C: population, territory, government and sovereignty
questions.D: land, labour, capital and enterprise
questions.explanation: Without any one of these a political community cannot be regarded as a state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A soldier forces villagers to hand over their farmland at gunpoint. The soldier is exercising
questions.A: legal-rational authority
questions.B: legitimate authority
questions.C: sovereignty
questions.D: power without authority
questions.explanation: Power is the ability to make others comply, by force if necessary; authority is power that is accepted as rightful.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A traditional ruler is obeyed by his people because his office has been passed down through generations. According to Max Weber, his authority is
questions.A: charismatic authority
questions.B: traditional authority
questions.C: legal-rational authority
questions.D: coercive authority
questions.explanation: Weber's three types are traditional (custom), charismatic (personal qualities) and legal-rational (rules and offices).

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Citizens obey a newly elected governor because the constitution gives him the office. This is an example of
questions.A: charismatic authority
questions.B: traditional authority
questions.C: legal-rational authority
questions.D: military power
questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority rests on laws and the office, not on the person or on custom.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A leader whose followers obey him because of his extraordinary personal qualities and vision possesses
questions.A: delegated authority
questions.B: traditional authority
questions.C: legal-rational authority
questions.D: charismatic authority
questions.explanation: Charismatic authority is based on devotion to the exceptional personality of the leader.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The supreme power of a state to make and enforce laws within its territory without external control is
questions.A: legitimacy
questions.B: sovereignty
questions.C: authority
questions.D: federalism
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the highest, final and absolute power of the state; internally it is supreme and externally it is independent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a democracy, legal sovereignty lies with the ______ while political sovereignty lies with the ______.
questions.A: president; judiciary
questions.B: electorate; law-making body
questions.C: law-making body; electorate
questions.D: army; civil service
questions.explanation: The legislature (or constitution) has the legal power to make binding laws, but the people who elect it are the ultimate political sovereign.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following limits the sovereignty of a modern state?
questions.A: the age of the country's constitution
questions.B: the size of the country's population
questions.C: the number of political parties in the country
questions.D: membership of international organisations such as the UN and ECOWAS
questions.explanation: Treaties and membership obligations restrict the freedom of action of states; public opinion and the constitution are internal limits.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A government that came to power through a coup later held elections, adopted a constitution and gained wide public acceptance. It acquired
questions.A: sovereignty
questions.B: legitimacy
questions.C: charisma
questions.D: immunity
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is popular acceptance of a government's right to rule; it can be gained through elections, good performance and constitutionalism.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The main difference between power and authority is that
questions.A: authority is always inherited, while power is always elected
questions.B: power is exercised only by governments, while authority is exercised by individuals
questions.C: authority is power that is recognised as rightful, while power may rest on force alone
questions.D: power is found only in democracies, while authority is found in monarchies
questions.explanation: Authority is legitimate power; naked power without acceptance is coercion.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A form of government in which the people rule either directly or through elected representatives is
questions.A: theocracy
questions.B: monarchy
questions.C: aristocracy
questions.D: democracy
questions.explanation: Democracy rests on popular sovereignty: government of the people, by the people and for the people.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In the ancient Greek city-state of Athens, citizens gathered in the assembly to make laws themselves. This is an example of
questions.A: representative democracy
questions.B: direct democracy
questions.C: constitutional monarchy
questions.D: oligarchy
questions.explanation: Direct democracy is possible only in small communities where all citizens can meet and decide.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Direct democracy is impracticable in modern Nigeria mainly because of
questions.A: the presence of a written constitution
questions.B: the existence of many political parties
questions.C: the large size of the population and territory
questions.D: the federal structure of the country
questions.explanation: Millions of citizens spread over a large area cannot assemble to decide every issue, so they elect representatives.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A government run by religious leaders who claim to rule according to divine law is
questions.A: a gerontocracy
questions.B: an aristocracy
questions.C: a plutocracy
questions.D: a theocracy
questions.explanation: Theocracy is rule by priests or clerics in the name of God, as in Iran after 1979 or the Sokoto Caliphate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A system in which the very rich control the government by virtue of their wealth is
questions.A: a theocracy
questions.B: a plutocracy
questions.C: a democracy
questions.D: a gerontocracy
questions.explanation: Plutocracy is rule by the wealthy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In many traditional African societies, the council of the oldest men took the most important decisions. This is
questions.A: theocracy
questions.B: plutocracy
questions.C: gerontocracy
questions.D: technocracy
questions.explanation: Gerontocracy is government by elders.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A king rules Saudi Arabia with wide personal powers, while the King of the United Kingdom reigns but does not rule. The two countries are respectively
questions.A: a theocracy and a republic
questions.B: a constitutional monarchy and an absolute monarchy
questions.C: a republic and a monarchy
questions.D: an absolute monarchy and a constitutional monarchy
questions.explanation: In an absolute monarchy the monarch's power is unlimited; in a constitutional monarchy real power lies with elected institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A republic differs from a monarchy in that in a republic the head of state is
questions.A: a hereditary ruler for life
questions.B: elected or chosen for a fixed period
questions.C: always a military officer
questions.D: appointed by religious leaders
questions.explanation: Nigeria became a republic in 1963 when an elected President replaced the Queen as head of state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A government in which one person seizes and holds power by force, ruling without constitutional limits, is
questions.A: a representative democracy
questions.B: a constitutional monarchy
questions.C: a dictatorship
questions.D: a federation
questions.explanation: Dictatorships concentrate absolute power in one person or a small clique and suppress opposition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Rule by the 'best' or by a privileged hereditary noble class is called
questions.A: anarchy
questions.B: democracy
questions.C: technocracy
questions.D: aristocracy
questions.explanation: Aristocracy literally means rule by the best; in practice it meant rule by a hereditary nobility.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A government of experts such as engineers, economists and scientists chosen for their technical knowledge is
questions.A: a plutocracy
questions.B: a technocracy
questions.C: a theocracy
questions.D: an autocracy
questions.explanation: Technocracy is rule by technical experts rather than by elected politicians.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A state in which the ruling party controls every aspect of public and private life through propaganda, a secret police and a single ideology is
questions.A: a constitutional monarchy
questions.B: democratic
questions.C: totalitarian
questions.D: a confederation
questions.explanation: Totalitarian regimes such as Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union sought total control over society.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A situation in which there is no government at all and no law and order is
questions.A: aristocracy
questions.B: autocracy
questions.C: oligarchy
questions.D: anarchy
questions.explanation: Anarchy is the absence of government; anarchists believe society can organise itself without the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The British Prime Minister is a member of the House of Commons and heads a cabinet drawn from Parliament. This fusion of the executive and the legislature is a feature of the
questions.A: presidential system
questions.B: parliamentary (cabinet) system
questions.C: confederal system
questions.D: unitary system
questions.explanation: In the parliamentary system the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under Nigeria's presidential system, a serving senator appointed as a minister must first
questions.A: be re-elected by his constituency
questions.B: obtain the permission of the Senate President
questions.C: resign his seat in the Senate
questions.D: be confirmed by the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: The presidential system separates personnel: no one may belong to both the executive and the legislature at the same time.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A vote of no confidence passed by parliament forces the prime minister and cabinet to resign. Such a vote is possible under the
questions.A: military system
questions.B: presidential system
questions.C: confederal system
questions.D: parliamentary system
questions.explanation: Because the cabinet depends on the confidence of parliament, losing a confidence vote ends its tenure.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of the presidential system over the parliamentary system is that
questions.A: the executive can be removed easily by the legislature
questions.B: the fixed term of the president provides stability
questions.C: it is cheaper to run because it has fewer officials
questions.D: the head of state and head of government are separate
questions.explanation: The president cannot be removed simply by losing a vote in the legislature, so governments are more stable.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A merit of the parliamentary system is that
questions.A: ministers are chosen from outside parliament on the basis of their technical expertise alone
questions.B: the president can ignore the wishes of the legislature once he has been elected for a fixed term
questions.C: the executive is continuously answerable to the legislature through question time and debates
questions.D: the head of state is directly elected by the whole country and cannot be removed by parliament
questions.explanation: Ministers must defend their policies in parliament daily, which makes government more responsive.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a parliamentary system, the head of state performs mainly ceremonial functions. In Nigeria's First Republic this role was played by the
questions.A: Speaker of the House of Representatives
questions.B: Prime Minister and the Federal Cabinet
questions.C: Chief Justice of the Federal Supreme Court
questions.D: Governor-General and later the President
questions.explanation: Nnamdi Azikiwe was ceremonial Governor-General from 1960 and ceremonial President from 1963, while Balewa held executive power as Prime Minister.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Individual ministerial responsibility means that a minister
questions.A: must support every decision of the cabinet in public even when he privately disagrees with it
questions.B: is answerable to parliament for the actions of his ministry and may resign over its failures
questions.C: can be removed from office only by the president and never by a vote of the legislature
questions.D: is personally responsible for the finances and staff of all the ministries of government
questions.explanation: Each minister answers personally for the conduct of his own department.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under the presidential system, ministers are appointed by the president and are responsible to
questions.A: the judiciary
questions.B: the legislature
questions.C: the president
questions.D: the electorate directly
questions.explanation: Ministers hold office at the pleasure of the president who appointed them, subject to legislative confirmation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In the presidential system the president is directly elected by the people, whereas in the parliamentary system the prime minister
questions.A: is chosen by the civil service
questions.B: is appointed by the chief justice
questions.C: is elected by the whole country in a separate ballot
questions.D: emerges as leader of the majority party or coalition in the legislature
questions.explanation: The prime minister is normally the leader of the party that commands a majority in the lower house.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A weakness of the parliamentary system is that
questions.A: the executive is too powerful to be checked by either the legislature or the courts
questions.B: governments can be unstable where many parties form shifting coalitions
questions.C: there is a complete separation of powers that prevents cooperation between the arms
questions.D: the head of government has a fixed term and cannot be removed before it expires
questions.explanation: Coalition governments can collapse whenever partners withdraw support, as happened often in Italy and the French Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In the presidential system the president combines the roles of
questions.A: head of government and speaker of the legislature
questions.B: head of state and chief justice
questions.C: head of state and head of government
questions.D: commander-in-chief and chief judge
questions.explanation: The president is both the ceremonial head of the nation and the chief executive.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Nigeria changed from the parliamentary system to the presidential system in
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution introduced an executive president modelled on the United States.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Switzerland is governed by a seven-member Federal Council that shares executive power. This is an example of a
questions.A: single executive
questions.B: plural executive
questions.C: parliamentary executive
questions.D: nominal executive
questions.explanation: In a plural (collegial) executive, power is shared among several persons of equal status.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Ghana's regions are administered by regional ministers appointed by the President and have no law-making powers of their own. Ghana operates
questions.A: a confederal system
questions.B: a federal system
questions.C: a unitary system
questions.D: a monarchical system
questions.explanation: In a unitary state all constitutional power belongs to the central government, which may delegate but not surrender it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of a federal system of government?
questions.A: a single legislature and a single judiciary that make and interpret laws for the whole country
questions.B: the concentration of all legislative and executive powers in the central government alone
questions.C: the right of the component units to secede from the union whenever they choose to do so
questions.D: a written constitution that divides powers between the central and component governments
questions.explanation: Federalism requires a written, rigid constitution that guarantees the powers of each level of government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Supreme Court of Nigeria settles disputes between the Federal Government and a state government. This shows that in a federation
questions.A: the central government is always superior to the states
questions.B: an independent judiciary interprets the division of powers
questions.C: states can ignore the decisions of the centre
questions.D: the legislature settles all constitutional disputes
questions.explanation: A neutral court is essential to resolve conflicts over the constitutional allocation of powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A unitary system is more suitable for a country that
questions.A: has strong regional identities
questions.B: is large and has many ethnic groups
questions.C: is small in size and has a homogeneous population
questions.D: was formed by the union of independent states
questions.explanation: Homogeneous, small countries such as Ghana and Britain do not need the power-sharing that diverse federations require.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of the unitary system of government is that
questions.A: it allows each region to have its own constitution
questions.B: it protects the identity of minority groups through regional autonomy
questions.C: it prevents the central government from becoming too powerful
questions.D: it avoids the duplication of government institutions and is cheaper to run
questions.explanation: One set of institutions serves the whole country, saving cost and simplifying decision-making.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A disadvantage of federalism is that
questions.A: power is concentrated in the central government
questions.B: it is expensive to run and may encourage sectional loyalties
questions.C: minority groups cannot be protected
questions.D: decisions are taken too quickly
questions.explanation: Duplicated institutions raise costs, and strong regional identities can threaten national unity.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a confederation, the member states
questions.A: have no governments of their own
questions.B: surrender all their powers to the central authority
questions.C: retain their sovereignty and can withdraw from the union
questions.D: are ruled directly by the central government
questions.explanation: Confederal central bodies are weak and depend on the member states, as in the Senegambia Confederation of 1982–1989.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Senegambia Confederation (1982–1989) collapsed mainly because
questions.A: the United Nations dissolved it
questions.B: the central government became too powerful
questions.C: the two countries were merged into one unitary state
questions.D: the member states retained their sovereignty and lost interest in the union
questions.explanation: Senegal and The Gambia kept separate governments and armies, and the loose union broke up when their interests diverged.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In Nigeria's federation, matters not listed in the exclusive or concurrent legislative lists are
questions.A: handled by the local governments alone
questions.B: residual matters reserved for the states
questions.C: decided by the Supreme Court
questions.D: reserved for the Federal Government
questions.explanation: Residual powers belong to the state Houses of Assembly.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Both the National Assembly and a state House of Assembly may make laws on post-primary education and electricity because these are on the
questions.A: residual list
questions.B: exclusive legislative list
questions.C: concurrent legislative list
questions.D: local government list
questions.explanation: Where both levels legislate on a concurrent matter and the laws conflict, the federal law prevails.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A federal system is usually adopted by a country in order to
questions.A: reduce the number of elections held and the cost of running government institutions
questions.B: make the central government all-powerful and remove the need for regional governments
questions.C: abolish the separate identities of its ethnic groups and create a single national culture
questions.D: keep a large and diverse country united while allowing regional self-rule
questions.explanation: Federalism balances unity with diversity, which is why large heterogeneous countries such as Nigeria, India and Canada adopt it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The devolution of powers to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has not made the United Kingdom a federation because
questions.A: each devolved region maintains its own army and conducts its own foreign policy
questions.B: the British Parliament can lawfully withdraw the devolved powers
questions.C: the regions can secede from the United Kingdom whenever their parliaments wish
questions.D: the monarch rules each region separately through appointed royal governors
questions.explanation: Devolved powers in a unitary state are delegated by the centre and can be revoked, unlike constitutionally guaranteed federal powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Nigeria's National Assembly consists of two chambers. This arrangement is described as
questions.A: federalism
questions.B: unicameralism
questions.C: bicameralism
questions.D: presidentialism
questions.explanation: The Senate and the House of Representatives together form a bicameral legislature.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of a bicameral legislature is that
questions.A: it gives the executive control of law-making
questions.B: laws are passed more quickly and cheaply
questions.C: it eliminates the need for committees
questions.D: the second chamber checks hasty legislation by the first
questions.explanation: A second chamber reviews bills and gives states or regions equal representation in a federation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Each Nigerian state is represented by three senators regardless of its population. This is intended to
questions.A: reward the states with the largest populations
questions.B: give the states equal representation in the federal legislature
questions.C: reduce the cost of running the Senate
questions.D: ensure that senators are elected by the state governors
questions.explanation: Equal representation in the upper house protects the interests of smaller states in a federation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The number of members of the Nigerian Senate is
questions.explanation: Three senators from each of the 36 states plus one from the Federal Capital Territory.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The House of Representatives in Nigeria has
questions.A: 774 members representing local government areas
questions.B: 109 members elected from the states
questions.C: 36 members representing the states
questions.D: 360 members elected from single-member constituencies
questions.explanation: Representation in the lower house is based on population, giving larger states more seats.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the legislature?
questions.A: making laws for the country
questions.B: interpreting the constitution in disputes
questions.C: approving the annual budget
questions.D: confirming appointments made by the executive
questions.explanation: Interpreting the constitution is the work of the judiciary.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The executive arm of government is responsible for
questions.A: interpreting laws and settling disputes
questions.B: making laws for the peace and good government of the country
questions.C: implementing laws and running the day-to-day administration of the state
questions.D: electing the members of the legislature
questions.explanation: The executive (president, ministers and the civil service) carries out the policies contained in the laws.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A court declares a law passed by the National Assembly null and void because it conflicts with the constitution. This power is called
questions.A: executive clemency
questions.B: judicial precedent
questions.C: legislative oversight
questions.D: judicial review
questions.explanation: Judicial review allows courts to test the actions of the other arms against the constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The independence of the judiciary in Nigeria is protected by
questions.A: the appointment of judges by the ruling party and their removal whenever the party loses power
questions.B: security of tenure for judges and payment of their salaries from the Consolidated Revenue Fund
questions.C: allowing judges to be removed by the president at will whenever their judgments displease him
questions.D: the payment of judges' salaries and allowances by the state governors from their security votes
questions.explanation: Judges cannot be removed without due process, and their salaries cannot be reduced by the executive.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The highest court in Nigeria is the
questions.A: Federal High Court
questions.B: Court of Appeal
questions.C: Supreme Court
questions.D: National Industrial Court
questions.explanation: Decisions of the Supreme Court are final and binding on all other courts.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The body responsible for recommending the appointment and discipline of judges in Nigeria is the
questions.A: Independent National Electoral Commission
questions.B: Federal Civil Service Commission
questions.C: Council of State
questions.D: National Judicial Council
questions.explanation: The NJC, headed by the Chief Justice, recommends judicial appointments to the President and governors.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A President grants pardon to a convicted prisoner. This is an exercise of
questions.A: judicial review
questions.B: the prerogative of mercy
questions.C: legislative oversight
questions.D: impeachment
questions.explanation: The prerogative of mercy allows the executive to pardon or reduce the sentences of convicted persons, after consulting the Council of State.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, the process of removing the President from office begins with a notice of allegation signed by at least
questions.A: a simple majority of the House of Representatives
questions.B: two-thirds of the members of the Senate
questions.C: one-third of the members of the National Assembly
questions.D: the Chief Justice of Nigeria
questions.explanation: The notice is followed by an investigation panel set up by the Chief Justice and a two-thirds vote of each house to remove.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The main function of the judiciary is to
questions.A: conduct elections
questions.B: make laws for the country
questions.C: implement government policies
questions.D: interpret the law and administer justice
questions.explanation: Courts settle disputes according to law and protect the rights of citizens.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Legislative oversight of the executive is exercised in Nigeria mainly through
questions.A: the appointment of ministers by the Senate President
questions.B: committees that investigate ministries and agencies
questions.C: the trial of ministers in the courts
questions.D: the election of the president by the legislature
questions.explanation: Standing committees summon officials, examine budgets and probe the use of public funds.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A constitution is best described as
questions.A: the manifesto of the ruling political party
questions.B: the list of laws passed by the legislature in a year
questions.C: the body of fundamental rules by which a state is governed
questions.D: the record of decisions of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: It defines the organs of government, their powers and the rights of citizens.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A written constitution is one which
questions.A: consists only of customs and conventions
questions.B: was written by foreign colonial officers
questions.C: cannot be amended by any means
questions.D: is contained in a single formal document
questions.explanation: Most countries, including Nigeria and the United States, have written constitutions; Britain's is unwritten.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a source of an unwritten constitution?
questions.A: a single document approved by referendum
questions.B: conventions, statutes, judicial decisions and customs
questions.C: the decrees of a military government
questions.D: the manifesto of the ruling party
questions.explanation: Britain's constitution is drawn from Acts of Parliament, court decisions, conventions and authoritative writings.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The practice that the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons becomes Prime Minister is a
questions.A: judicial precedent
questions.B: statute law
questions.C: constitutional convention
questions.D: royal decree
questions.explanation: Conventions are unwritten but binding practices that fill gaps in the constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The supremacy of the constitution means that
questions.A: the legislature is above the constitution
questions.B: the president can override the constitution in an emergency
questions.C: the constitution can be changed by a simple majority
questions.D: any law inconsistent with the constitution is void to the extent of the inconsistency
questions.explanation: Section 1 of the 1999 Constitution declares it supreme and binding on all authorities and persons.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A merit of a rigid constitution is that it
questions.A: can be adapted quickly to changing circumstances
questions.B: protects fundamental rights and the federal structure from hasty change
questions.C: does not require a special amendment procedure
questions.D: gives the government unlimited powers
questions.explanation: Special majorities make it difficult for a temporary majority to alter basic arrangements.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A disadvantage of a rigid constitution is that it
questions.A: gives too much power to the courts
questions.B: is easily changed by the ruling party
questions.C: may be difficult to adapt to changing needs
questions.D: cannot protect minority rights
questions.explanation: Cumbersome amendment procedures can leave outdated provisions in force for long periods.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following countries has a flexible constitution?
questions.A: Australia
questions.B: Nigeria
questions.C: the United States
questions.D: the United Kingdom
questions.explanation: The British Parliament can change any constitutional rule by an ordinary Act.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The preamble to a constitution
questions.A: lists the powers of the local governments
questions.B: states the aims and aspirations of the people who adopt it
questions.C: contains the details of the electoral system
questions.D: is the most important enforceable section
questions.explanation: The preamble ('We the people...') sets out the purposes of the constitution but is not itself enforceable law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy in Chapter II of the 1999 Constitution
questions.A: list the exclusive legislative powers
questions.B: can be enforced by any citizen in the High Court
questions.C: guide government policy but are not enforceable in court
questions.D: define who is a citizen of Nigeria
questions.explanation: Section 6(6)(c) makes Chapter II non-justiciable, unlike the fundamental rights in Chapter IV.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a function of a constitution?
questions.A: settling commercial disputes between traders and their customers in the market
questions.B: increasing the revenue of the government through the collection of taxes and levies
questions.C: choosing the members of the cabinet and allocating ministries among them
questions.D: limiting the powers of government and protecting the rights of citizens
questions.explanation: Constitutions define, distribute and limit power and set out citizens' rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: To amend most sections of the 1999 Constitution, a proposal must be supported by
questions.A: a simple majority of the members of the Senate and the assent of the President within thirty days
questions.B: two-thirds of each house of the National Assembly and two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly
questions.C: the President, the Chief Justice of Nigeria and a majority of the members of the Council of State
questions.D: a referendum in which more than half of all the registered voters in the country approve the change
questions.explanation: Section 9 requires two-thirds of each house and approval by at least 24 of the 36 state assemblies; some sections need four-fifths.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A constitution that provides for a head of state who is not a hereditary ruler is described as
questions.A: confederal
questions.B: monarchical
questions.C: republican
questions.D: unitary
questions.explanation: Nigeria's 1963 Constitution made the country a republic with a President as head of state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The doctrine of separation of powers is associated with the French philosopher
questions.A: A. V. Dicey
questions.B: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
questions.C: Karl Marx
questions.D: Baron de Montesquieu
questions.explanation: Montesquieu developed the doctrine in The Spirit of the Laws (1748).

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The main purpose of the separation of powers is to
questions.A: make government faster and more efficient by removing the need for consultation between arms
questions.B: prevent the concentration of power in one person or body and so protect liberty
questions.C: give the executive full control over the courts so that judgments support government policy
questions.D: allow the legislature to implement its own laws without depending on the executive to do so
questions.explanation: Montesquieu argued that when legislative, executive and judicial powers are united, tyranny follows.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under Nigeria's presidential system, the President appoints judges but only on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council and with the confirmation of the Senate. This illustrates
questions.A: fusion of powers
questions.B: complete separation of powers
questions.C: checks and balances
questions.D: delegated legislation
questions.explanation: Each arm takes part in and limits the actions of the others so that no arm acts alone.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The principle of the rule of law was popularised by
questions.A: Thomas Hobbes
questions.B: Montesquieu
questions.C: John Locke
questions.D: A. V. Dicey
questions.explanation: Dicey set out the doctrine in his Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885).

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: According to Dicey, one of the principles of the rule of law is that
questions.A: the president and his ministers are above the law for as long as they remain in office
questions.B: no one should be punished except for a breach of law established in the ordinary courts
questions.C: the government may detain citizens without trial whenever it considers this to be necessary
questions.D: laws should apply differently to the rich and the poor according to their position in society
questions.explanation: Dicey's principles are supremacy of the law, equality before the law and protection of rights through the courts.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution, which shields the President and governors from court action while in office, is a limitation on
questions.A: the supremacy of the constitution
questions.B: the separation of powers
questions.C: the rule of law
questions.D: federalism
questions.explanation: Immunity clauses conflict with the principle that all persons are equal before the law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a limitation on the rule of law?
questions.A: the holding of periodic free and fair elections
questions.B: the independence of the judiciary from the executive
questions.C: the right of every accused person to a fair hearing
questions.D: diplomatic immunity enjoyed by foreign ambassadors
questions.explanation: Diplomats cannot be tried in the courts of the host country, an exception to equality before the law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The declaration of a state of emergency limits the rule of law because
questions.A: the courts stop functioning permanently
questions.B: some fundamental rights may be suspended
questions.C: the constitution is abolished
questions.D: the legislature is dissolved for ever
questions.explanation: During an emergency, rights such as freedom of movement may be lawfully restricted.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following best describes constitutionalism?
questions.A: the amendment of the constitution by the legislature
questions.B: the possession of a written constitution by a country
questions.C: government conducted according to the limits laid down in the constitution
questions.D: rule by decree during military government
questions.explanation: A country may have a constitution without constitutionalism if rulers ignore its limits.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Periodic elections are essential to democracy because they
questions.A: remove the need for a constitution
questions.B: guarantee that the same party remains in power
questions.C: reduce the cost of running government
questions.D: enable citizens to choose and change their rulers peacefully
questions.explanation: Regular elections make governments accountable to the people.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The principle that the party with the most votes forms the government while the rights of the minority are respected is
questions.A: the doctrine of separation of powers
questions.B: majority rule with minority rights
questions.C: the principle of the rule of law
questions.D: the federal character principle
questions.explanation: Democracy is not merely majority rule; the losers retain their rights and can compete again.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of a democratic government?
questions.A: life tenure for the head of state
questions.B: a single political party permitted by law
questions.C: freedom of the press and association
questions.D: elections held at the pleasure of the ruler
questions.explanation: Free media and the right to form associations allow citizens to hold government to account.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The definition of democracy as 'government of the people, by the people and for the people' was given by
questions.A: Nnamdi Azikiwe
questions.B: Winston Churchill
questions.C: Karl Marx
questions.D: Abraham Lincoln
questions.explanation: Lincoln used the phrase in his Gettysburg Address of 1863.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The delegation of law-making powers to ministers and agencies is regarded as a threat to the rule of law because
questions.A: ministers are never permitted to make rules of any kind under the constitution
questions.B: rules are made by bodies that are not directly elected and with less scrutiny
questions.C: the courts have no power whatsoever to review or strike down delegated legislation
questions.D: it abolishes the legislature and transfers all its law-making functions to the executive
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation is often made without full debate, though it remains subject to judicial review.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An independent electoral body is important in a democracy because it
questions.A: decides which laws the legislature should pass and which policies the executive should adopt
questions.B: chooses the candidates that all the political parties must present at every election
questions.C: ensures that elections are conducted fairly without control by the government in power
questions.D: appoints the judges of the election tribunals and decides the outcome of election petitions
questions.explanation: If the ruling party controlled elections, opposition parties could not compete on equal terms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, a person born in Nigeria before independence whose parent or grandparent belonged to an indigenous Nigerian community is a citizen
questions.A: by honour
questions.B: by registration
questions.C: by naturalisation
questions.D: by birth
questions.explanation: Citizenship by birth is based on descent from indigenous Nigerian communities or from Nigerian parents.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A foreign woman married to a Nigerian man applies to become a Nigerian. If granted, she becomes a citizen
questions.A: by naturalisation
questions.B: by registration
questions.C: by birth
questions.D: by adoption
questions.explanation: Section 26 allows registration of a woman married to a Nigerian citizen and of persons of full age with Nigerian grandparents.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: To qualify for citizenship by naturalisation in Nigeria, an applicant must, among other things, have resided in Nigeria continuously for
questions.A: two years
questions.B: five years
questions.C: fifteen years
questions.D: twenty-five years
questions.explanation: Section 27 requires fifteen years' continuous residence (or an aggregate of fifteen years within twenty), good character and acceptability to the local community.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A Nigerian citizen by naturalisation may be deprived of his citizenship if he
questions.A: travels abroad for a holiday lasting more than three months without informing the government
questions.B: changes his religion or joins a political party different from the one in government
questions.C: marries a foreigner and brings his spouse to live with him permanently in Nigeria
questions.D: is convicted and sentenced to three years' imprisonment within seven years of naturalisation
questions.explanation: Section 30 permits deprivation of registered or naturalised citizens for disloyalty or serious crime; citizens by birth cannot be deprived.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a fundamental right guaranteed in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.A: the right to free university education
questions.B: the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion
questions.C: the right to a job in the civil service
questions.D: the right to a house provided by government
questions.explanation: Chapter IV covers civil and political rights; education and housing are directive principles in Chapter II.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A citizen whose fundamental right has been violated may seek redress in the
questions.A: police station only
questions.B: local government council
questions.C: High Court
questions.D: National Assembly
questions.explanation: Section 46 gives the High Court original jurisdiction over applications to enforce fundamental rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a duty of a citizen of Nigeria under Section 24 of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.A: to attend a university
questions.B: to belong to a political party
questions.C: to serve in the armed forces for life
questions.D: to pay taxes promptly and honestly
questions.explanation: Duties include respecting the national symbols, helping law enforcement, paying taxes and protecting public property.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A citizen may lawfully lose his Nigerian citizenship by
questions.A: changing his surname
questions.B: renunciation
questions.C: failing to vote in an election
questions.D: living in another state
questions.explanation: Section 29 allows a citizen of full age to renounce his citizenship by declaration.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The right to vote and be voted for is classified as a
questions.A: social right
questions.B: economic right
questions.C: political right
questions.D: natural right
questions.explanation: Political rights concern participation in the government of the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a way of acquiring Nigerian citizenship under the 1999 Constitution?
questions.A: by naturalisation
questions.B: by birth
questions.C: by registration
questions.D: by purchase
questions.explanation: Citizenship cannot be bought; the constitution recognises only birth, registration and naturalisation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A Nigerian citizen by birth who also acquires the citizenship of another country
questions.A: automatically loses his Nigerian citizenship
questions.B: retains his Nigerian citizenship
questions.C: becomes a citizen by naturalisation
questions.D: must renounce one within a year
questions.explanation: Section 28 forbids dual citizenship only for citizens by registration or naturalisation, not for citizens by birth.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The main difference between a citizen and an alien is that a citizen
questions.A: is exempted from paying taxes
questions.B: cannot be tried in the courts of the state
questions.C: enjoys full political rights and owes allegiance to the state
questions.D: must belong to the ruling party
questions.explanation: Aliens may live and work in a country but cannot vote or hold most public offices.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Communist Manifesto of 1848 was written by
questions.A: Lenin and Stalin
questions.B: Adam Smith and David Ricardo
questions.C: John Locke and Thomas Hobbes
questions.D: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels called on the workers of the world to unite and overthrow capitalism.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The ideology which holds that the means of production should be owned by the community and that class differences should be abolished is
questions.A: capitalism
questions.B: communism
questions.C: fascism
questions.D: feudalism
questions.explanation: Communism envisages a classless, stateless society in which property is held in common.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In the ideology of Karl Marx, the class struggle in capitalist society is between
questions.A: farmers and traders
questions.B: the clergy and the nobility
questions.C: the bourgeoisie and the proletariat
questions.D: civilians and soldiers
questions.explanation: The bourgeoisie own the means of production while the proletariat sell their labour.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Mussolini's Italy and Hitler's Germany were governed according to
questions.A: feudalism
questions.B: communism
questions.C: liberal democracy
questions.D: fascism
questions.explanation: Fascism glorifies the nation and the leader, rejects democracy and suppresses opposition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In medieval Europe, lords granted land to vassals in return for military service while serfs worked the land. This system was
questions.A: capitalism
questions.B: feudalism
questions.C: socialism
questions.D: communism
questions.explanation: Feudalism was based on land ownership and personal obligations between lords and their dependants.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Democratic socialism differs from communism in that democratic socialists
questions.A: support the private ownership of all industries
questions.B: advocate violent revolution
questions.C: seek to achieve their goals through elections and parliamentary reform
questions.D: reject the idea of social welfare
questions.explanation: Democratic socialists accept multi-party democracy and gradual change, unlike revolutionary communists.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Socialism differs from capitalism mainly in that under socialism
questions.A: the church controls economic life
questions.B: individuals own property and compete for profit
questions.C: there is no government at all
questions.D: the major means of production are owned by the state or the community
questions.explanation: Socialism stresses collective ownership and equality; capitalism stresses private ownership and the market.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A state that provides free health care, unemployment benefits and pensions for all its citizens, financed by taxation, is practising
questions.A: fascism
questions.B: welfarism
questions.C: feudalism
questions.D: anarchism
questions.explanation: The welfare state uses public resources to guarantee a minimum standard of living.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The ideology that stresses individual freedom, limited government and equality before the law is
questions.A: fascism
questions.B: totalitarianism
questions.C: liberalism
questions.D: feudalism
questions.explanation: Liberalism grew out of the writings of John Locke and others who defended individual rights against the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An ideology that favours the preservation of traditional institutions and gradual rather than radical change is
questions.A: radicalism
questions.B: communism
questions.C: anarchism
questions.D: conservatism
questions.explanation: Conservatives value continuity, order and established institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Nationalism as an ideology emphasises
questions.A: the abolition of all states and national boundaries in favour of world government
questions.B: loyalty to one's nation and its right to self-determination
questions.C: the common ownership of property and the abolition of social classes
questions.D: loyalty to a religious leader above loyalty to any country or government
questions.explanation: Nationalism inspired the anti-colonial movements that won independence for African states.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following was a feature of the Soviet Union under communism?
questions.A: private ownership of all major industries
questions.B: free multi-party elections every four years
questions.C: a one-party state with a centrally planned economy
questions.D: a hereditary monarchy
questions.explanation: The Communist Party monopolised power and the state owned and planned the economy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Anarchism as a political ideology advocates
questions.A: government by religious leaders
questions.B: rule by a strong dictator
questions.C: the ownership of all property by the state
questions.D: the abolition of the state and all forms of coercive authority
questions.explanation: Anarchists regard the state as unnecessary and oppressive and favour voluntary cooperation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A proposed law presented to the legislature for consideration is called
questions.A: an act
questions.B: a bill
questions.C: a decree
questions.D: a motion
questions.explanation: A bill becomes an Act (law) after passing all stages and receiving assent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: At the first reading of a bill in the National Assembly,
questions.A: the bill is sent to the President for assent
questions.B: the bill is debated clause by clause
questions.C: the title of the bill is read and no debate takes place
questions.D: members vote on the principles of the bill
questions.explanation: The first reading is a formal introduction; debate on principles comes at the second reading.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A senator rises to argue that a bill on electricity tariffs is unnecessary in principle, without discussing any of its clauses. This debate takes place at the
questions.A: report stage
questions.B: first reading
questions.C: committee stage
questions.D: second reading
questions.explanation: Members decide at the second reading whether the bill deserves further consideration.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The stage at which a bill is examined in detail and amendments are made to its clauses is the
questions.A: first reading
questions.B: committee stage
questions.C: second reading
questions.D: third reading
questions.explanation: A committee of the house scrutinises the bill line by line.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: After the committee stage, the committee's amendments are reported to the whole house at the
questions.A: second reading
questions.B: first reading
questions.C: report stage
questions.D: assent stage
questions.explanation: The house considers the committee's report before the final (third) reading.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a bicameral legislature, a bill passed by one chamber must
questions.A: be published in a national newspaper for one year before it becomes law
questions.B: be signed immediately by the president without any further consideration
questions.C: be approved by the Supreme Court before it can be presented for assent
questions.D: also be passed by the other chamber before it is sent for assent
questions.explanation: Both chambers must pass identical versions; a conference committee reconciles differences.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A bill that seeks to raise revenue or authorise government spending is called
questions.A: a private bill
questions.B: a money (appropriation) bill
questions.C: a hybrid bill
questions.D: a constitutional bill
questions.explanation: Money bills are normally introduced by the executive and must pass through the legislature before public funds are spent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A bill that affects only a particular person, group or locality rather than the whole country is
questions.A: a money bill
questions.B: a public bill
questions.C: a private bill
questions.D: a government bill
questions.explanation: Private bills deal with specific interests, such as the incorporation of a particular body.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The last stage before a bill passed by both houses becomes law in Nigeria is
questions.A: publication in the gazette
questions.B: the third reading
questions.C: the committee stage
questions.D: the President's assent
questions.explanation: Assent by the President (or governor for state bills) turns the bill into an Act.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: If the President neither signs a bill nor communicates his refusal within thirty days, the National Assembly
questions.A: must abandon the bill completely and may not reintroduce it during that legislative session
questions.B: may pass it again by a two-thirds majority and it becomes law without assent
questions.C: must send the bill to the Supreme Court, which decides whether it should become law
questions.D: must hold a national referendum in which the electorate decides whether to accept the bill
questions.explanation: Section 58 of the 1999 Constitution allows the legislature to override a veto or inaction by two-thirds of each house.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Regulations made by a minister under powers given by an Act of the National Assembly are called
questions.A: constitutional amendments
questions.B: private members' bills
questions.C: delegated (subsidiary) legislation
questions.D: judicial precedents
questions.explanation: Parliament delegates detailed rule-making because it lacks the time and technical expertise to cover every detail.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The presiding officer of the House of Representatives in Nigeria is the
questions.A: Majority Leader
questions.B: Senate President
questions.C: Clerk
questions.D: Speaker
questions.explanation: The Speaker is elected by the members from among themselves at the first sitting.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a constituency election, Candidate X scored 45%, Y 30% and Z 25% and X was declared the winner. The rule under which X won is the
questions.A: absolute majority system
questions.B: simple majority (first-past-the-post) system
questions.C: proportional representation system
questions.D: second ballot system
questions.explanation: Under first-past-the-post the candidate with the most votes wins even without more than half of the votes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of the simple majority electoral system is that it
questions.A: prevents wasted votes
questions.B: gives every party seats in proportion to its votes
questions.C: is simple to operate and usually produces a clear winner
questions.D: guarantees the representation of minority parties
questions.explanation: It is easy to understand and count and tends to produce stable single-party governments.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A disadvantage of the simple majority system is that
questions.A: it requires a second round of voting
questions.B: it is too complicated for voters to understand
questions.C: it always produces coalition governments
questions.D: a candidate can win with far less than half of the votes cast
questions.explanation: Votes for losing candidates are wasted, and the winner may lack majority support.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In an election, a party that won 30% of the national vote received 30% of the seats in parliament. The electoral system used was
questions.A: simple majority
questions.B: proportional representation
questions.C: absolute majority
questions.D: second ballot
questions.explanation: Proportional representation allocates seats in proportion to votes, often using party lists.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In France, if no presidential candidate wins more than half of the votes, a second round is held between the two leading candidates. This is the
questions.A: list system
questions.B: first-past-the-post system
questions.C: second ballot (run-off) system
questions.D: single transferable vote system
questions.explanation: The second ballot ensures the winner has an absolute majority in the final round.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The President of the United States is formally chosen by
questions.A: the Supreme Court
questions.B: a direct national vote alone
questions.C: the Senate
questions.D: an electoral college
questions.explanation: Voters choose electors in each state, and the electors elect the President.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The minimum voting age in Nigeria is
questions.A: 21 years
questions.B: 18 years
questions.C: 16 years
questions.D: 25 years
questions.explanation: Every Nigerian who has attained the age of 18 is entitled to be registered as a voter.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Universal adult suffrage means that
questions.A: only adult men who have completed military service have the right to vote
questions.B: only citizens who pay taxes and own property have the right to vote in elections
questions.C: all adult citizens have the right to vote regardless of sex, wealth or education
questions.D: only literate citizens who can read the ballot paper have the right to vote
questions.explanation: Every citizen aged 18 and above may vote, whatever their sex, wealth, religion or level of education.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A group of voters signs a petition to remove their senator before the end of his term. This process is called
questions.A: plebiscite
questions.B: impeachment
questions.C: referendum
questions.D: recall
questions.explanation: Section 69 of the 1999 Constitution allows recall by a petition signed by more than half of the registered voters in the constituency.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The deliberate drawing of constituency boundaries to favour a particular party is called
questions.A: delimitation
questions.B: gerrymandering
questions.C: rigging
questions.D: lobbying
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering manipulates boundaries so that a party's supporters are concentrated or spread to its advantage.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a form of electoral malpractice?
questions.A: accrediting voters with a card reader
questions.B: counting votes in the presence of party agents
questions.C: stuffing ballot boxes with pre-marked ballot papers
questions.D: announcing results at the polling unit
questions.explanation: Ballot stuffing, multiple voting, vote buying and falsification of results are all forms of rigging.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Nigeria's Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced mainly to
questions.A: replace the voters' register with party membership cards
questions.B: allow Nigerians abroad to vote by post
questions.C: count votes automatically without human involvement
questions.D: verify voters' identity by fingerprint or face and reduce multiple voting
questions.explanation: BVAS accredits voters biometrically and uploads polling-unit results, reducing impersonation and inflated figures.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Independent National Electoral Commission is empowered to do all of the following EXCEPT
questions.A: register political parties and monitor their finances
questions.B: try and punish persons who commit electoral offences
questions.C: register voters and maintain the register of voters
questions.D: divide the country into constituencies for elections
questions.explanation: Trial and punishment of offenders is the function of the courts, not INEC.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A disputed election result in Nigeria is challenged first at
questions.A: the Senate
questions.B: the Supreme Court
questions.C: an election petition tribunal
questions.D: the police headquarters
questions.explanation: Election tribunals hear petitions, with appeals to the Court of Appeal and, for presidential elections, the Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Secret ballot is important in elections because it
questions.A: allows voters to sell their votes safely
questions.B: makes counting faster
questions.C: reduces the number of candidates
questions.D: protects voters from intimidation and victimisation
questions.explanation: When no one can see how a voter voted, employers, parties and thugs cannot punish them for their choice.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The single transferable vote is a form of proportional representation in which voters
questions.A: vote for a single party list only
questions.B: rank candidates in order of preference in multi-member constituencies
questions.C: vote twice in two rounds
questions.D: choose one candidate in a single-member constituency
questions.explanation: Surplus votes of elected candidates and votes of eliminated candidates are transferred according to the voters' preferences.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A political party is best defined as
questions.A: an association of traders in a market
questions.B: a group that influences government without seeking office
questions.C: an organised group of people seeking to capture and exercise governmental power
questions.D: a body that conducts elections
questions.explanation: The desire to win power through elections distinguishes parties from pressure groups.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Which of the following is a function of political parties?
questions.A: collecting taxes from members of the public
questions.B: conducting and supervising elections
questions.C: interpreting the constitution
questions.D: recruiting and presenting candidates for elections
questions.explanation: Parties also educate voters, aggregate interests and form the government or the opposition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under the Babangida transition programme, only the SDP and NRC were allowed to exist. Nigeria then operated
questions.A: a multi-party system chosen by the people
questions.B: a two-party system imposed by decree
questions.C: a one-party system imposed by decree
questions.D: a no-party system with independent candidates
questions.explanation: The two parties were created by the military government in 1989 for the Third Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of the two-party system is that it
questions.A: removes the need for elections
questions.B: gives every shade of opinion a party
questions.C: usually produces a stable government with a clear opposition
questions.D: prevents the formation of any opposition
questions.explanation: One party normally wins a clear majority while the other provides an alternative government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: An advantage of the multi-party system is that it
questions.A: prevents ethnic and religious parties from forming in a divided society
questions.B: always produces a single-party majority and a strong, stable government
questions.C: eliminates the need for coalition governments after every election
questions.D: gives a wide range of interests and opinions representation
questions.explanation: Many parties allow minorities and diverse views to be represented, though governments may be less stable.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A party whose membership is open to all and which relies on large numbers of ordinary members for funds and support is
questions.A: an elite (cadre) party
questions.B: a mass party
questions.C: a broker party
questions.D: a charismatic party
questions.explanation: Mass parties such as the NCNC and the Action Group sought members across whole regions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A party built around the personality of a single popular leader is
questions.A: a mass party
questions.B: an ideological party
questions.C: a charismatic party
questions.D: a cadre party
questions.explanation: Such parties often decline when the leader leaves the scene.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: In a one-party state, elections
questions.A: are conducted by the opposition parties under the supervision of the courts
questions.B: are held every year so that the people can change the government
questions.C: are always free and fair because there is no competition to rig them
questions.D: offer voters no real choice between competing parties
questions.explanation: With only one legal party, voters can at most choose between candidates of the same party.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A political party's manifesto is important because it
questions.A: lists the names and addresses of all the registered members of the party
questions.B: tells voters the policies the party will implement if elected
questions.C: is the constitution of the country and binds all the other parties as well
questions.D: is the document the electoral commission uses to conduct the election
questions.explanation: The manifesto allows voters to compare parties and hold the winner to its promises.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: After losing a general election, a party's legislators sit on the minority benches and question the budget line by line. In doing so they are performing the opposition's duty to
questions.A: share ministerial posts with the ruling party
questions.B: obstruct every action of the government by force
questions.C: criticise the government and offer alternative policies
questions.D: conduct the next general election
questions.explanation: A responsible opposition holds the government to account and stands ready to replace it.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A coalition government is formed when
questions.A: the president appoints ministers from his own party only
questions.B: one party wins all the seats in parliament
questions.C: the military hands over to civilians
questions.D: two or more parties share power because no party has a majority
questions.explanation: Coalitions are common under proportional representation and in multi-party systems.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Under the 1999 Constitution, a political party in Nigeria must
questions.A: restrict its membership to one ethnic group so that it can represent that group properly
questions.B: have its headquarters in the Federal Capital Territory and be open to all Nigerians
questions.C: be registered by the Senate and have its constitution approved by the Supreme Court
questions.D: have a religious name and symbol that reflects the faith of the majority of its members
questions.explanation: Section 222 requires national spread, open membership and a headquarters in Abuja; ethnic or religious names are forbidden.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Party discipline is enforced in the legislature by
questions.A: the chief justice
questions.B: the clerk of the house
questions.C: the party whip
questions.D: the electoral commission
questions.explanation: Whips ensure that party members attend and vote according to the party line.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria lobbies the government for lower import duties on raw materials. MAN is
questions.A: an anomic group
questions.B: a political party
questions.C: a promotional pressure group
questions.D: an economic (interest) pressure group
questions.explanation: Economic or occupational groups defend the material interests of their members.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: A group formed to campaign for the protection of the environment, whose members gain no personal benefit, is
questions.A: a promotional (cause) group
questions.B: an occupational group
questions.C: a political party
questions.D: an institutional group
questions.explanation: Promotional groups pursue a cause or principle rather than the interests of members.

questions.subject: Government
questions.q: Angry youths spontaneously block a highway to protest the killing of a trader by security operatives. Such a group is
questions.A: an anomic pressure group
questions.B: an institutional pressure group
questions.C: an associational pressure group
questions.D: a political party
questions.explanation: Anomic groups are spontaneous, unorganised and short-lived, often arising from sudden grievance.
